description: We are E.T., a group of friends passionate about using technology to tackle real-world challenges. Through our project, TERRA, we use NASA satellite and climate data to help farmers make informed decisions about crop rotation, water conservation, and soil health. By combining our interests in computer science, space technology, and sustainability, we hope to make complex scientific data accessible and empower communities to build a more resilient future.
summary:
Arizona farmers are losing canal water. Their wells are dropping. The heat keeps rising. Choosing what to plant next has become a gamble. TERRA (Transforming Earth Research into Resilient Agriculture), built by Team E.T., is a free app that helps a farmer make that choice for their own field.

The farmer picks their field on a map and enters what they grow and how much water they get. TERRA then tests over 12,000 three-year crop rotations against 20 years of NASA POWER weather for that exact spot, replaying each plan year by year. It suggests four plans, called Most income, Least water, Best for soil and Safest in dry years. Each one shows how much water it saves and whether it makes or loses money. Farmers can also see how a plan would do if canal water is cut again.

We checked TERRA against real measurements from 12 Arizona weather stations, and its estimates of how much water crops need were within about 5% on average. TERRA also uses NASA satellite images to see whether the field is actually green when the farmer says a crop is growing. State well records show how quickly the water underground is dropping near each farm. Every plan tells the farmer how sure TERRA is about it and explains why in plain words.

TERRA works anywhere on Earth, but it goes deepest in Arizona, where a dry future is our present reality. It is available in English and Spanish on the ground.
details:
The Problem
Farming in Arizona keeps getting harder. On January 1, 2023, farmers in Pinal County lost the last of their Colorado River water from the Central Arizona Project canal. Many switched to pumping groundwater, and the water table under them is now dropping year after year. Summers are getting hotter as well. Near Casa Grande, the number of days over 110°F went from about 20 a year to about 29 within a decade.

A farmer in this position has to decide what to plant without knowing how much water they will have. Planting the same crop every year wears out the soil. Planting by habit is risky when the weather keeps breaking records. NASA has decades of data that could help, but it is not in a form a farmer can use to make a planting decision.

What TERRA Does
TERRA is a free website that recommends crop plans for one specific field. It looks at that field’s weather, soil and water supply, and tells the farmer which crops to grow over the next three years and why.

The farmer starts by finding their field on a satellite map, or by choosing one of four Arizona demo farms. Next they tap in what they plan to grow, season by season, for three years. Finally they set how much water they get, whether it comes from wells or the canal, what they pay for it, and how they irrigate. Crops a farmer can’t grow or sell can be left out, and every setting can be changed later.

TERRA then tests over 12,000 possible three-year crop rotations against that field’s real weather for every year from 2005 to 2024. It shows four plans next to what the farmer grows now. One earns the most money, one uses the least water, one is best for the soil, and one holds up best in dry years. Each plan shows how many gallons of water it saves out of the total, whether it makes or loses money per acre, and how many of the last 20 years it would have fit within the farmer’s water supply.

A Real Example
Take a demo field near Casa Grande that gets 4.1 acre-feet of water per acre. Growing alfalfa there every year needs about 1.8 million gallons per acre a year. That is more water than the field gets, so in all 20 years the crop comes up short and the farmer loses about $413 per acre. TERRA’s “Safest in dry years” plan grows guar and sesame instead. It uses about 0.5 million gallons, fits the water supply in all 20 years, and earns about $128 per acre.

The Data Behind It

  • NASA POWER: 20 years of daily weather for the exact field, including heat, humidity, wind, sunlight and rain. This is the core of every water estimate.
  • NASA MODIS Terra satellite images (through NASA GIBS): a measure of how green the field is, every 16 days.
  • NASA SMAP and GRACE-FO: soil moisture and underground water shown on the field map.
  • AZMET weather stations (University of Arizona): used to test how accurate TERRA’s water estimates are.
  • Arizona Department of Water Resources: state well records and the boundaries of groundwater management areas.
  • ISRIC SoilGrids: the soil makeup at each field.
  • USDA and University of Arizona: Arizona crop yields, prices and the cost of growing each crop.

How It Works
To estimate how much water a crop needs, TERRA uses the FAO-56 method from the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization, the standard used around the world. It first works out how much water the air pulls from the ground each day, then adjusts that for each crop as it grows. Rain that soaks in is subtracted using the USDA’s standard method. The result is adjusted for how efficient the farmer’s irrigation is, roughly 70% for furrow and 90% for drip.

TERRA follows real farming rules when it builds rotations. For instance, crops are only planted in their season, cotton has to go in by April, and frost and heat limits are respected. Each rotation is scored on water use, soil health, how it does in dry years, and income. Rather than handing over a single score, TERRA explains what each plan does well and where it falls short. It also says how confident it is in each plan.

What Makes TERRA Different

We checked it against real weather stations. We compared TERRA’s water estimates with measurements from 12 AZMET weather stations across Arizona from 2020 to 2024. When testing each station, we tuned TERRA without that station’s data, so every result comes from a place the model had never seen. TERRA came within 4.8% on average, more accurate than the standard textbook formula, which was off by 7.2%. TERRA uses whichever method works better for a field and tells the user which one it chose.

It replays real years, not an average one. Most tools plan for a typical year. TERRA runs each plan through all 20 years from 2005 to 2024, one at a time. Each year is marked green if the plan stayed within the water supply, yellow if it was close, and red if it ran out. This shows whether a plan only works in a good year or holds up in the bad ones.

It checks what the satellite actually sees. TERRA reads NASA’s MODIS satellite images of the field and measures how green it is through the year. If the farmer says a crop is growing but the field looks bare from space, TERRA points it out and asks them to check.

It shows the groundwater picture. TERRA uses 20 to 49 state monitoring wells near each demo farm, some with records back to 1995, to show how fast the water underground is dropping. It uses a trend method that one strange reading can’t throw off. It also tells the farmer whether their field falls inside a groundwater management area with pumping limits, including the new Willcox and Ranegras Plain areas.

It plans for canal cuts. Every plan is tested three ways: with full canal water, with the 2022 Colorado River cut, and with no canal water at all. That is the situation Pinal farmers actually faced.

It shows the money. Profit or loss per acre comes from University of Arizona crop budgets, USDA Arizona prices and yields, and the farmer’s own water price. When a plan doesn’t get enough water, TERRA lowers the expected harvest using the FAO’s published yield loss factors for each crop.

It knows when heat hurts the crop. Using AZMET’s cotton heat stress records, we built a model that estimates how hot the cotton plants themselves get, based on NASA weather. TERRA counts the July and August days when the plants pass 82°F, the point where University of Arizona research shows young cotton bolls start to fall off.

Farmers can also try their own plans in Build, swap any crop, and see the effect right away. Plans can be saved to My farm, which shows the 7-day forecast and any National Weather Service warnings for that location.

Tools and Technology
TERRA is written in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. All the crop calculations run inside the user’s browser, in the background, so the screen never freezes. The map uses MapLibre GL. Live data comes from NASA POWER, NASA GIBS, SoilGrids, Open-Meteo and the National Weather Service. We wrote Node.js and Python scripts to prepare the NASA, AZMET, ADWR and SoilGrids data for the demo farms. Automated tests run on every update to make sure the water estimates and crop rules are still right.

The site is hosted on GitHub Pages and at apptera.earth, and the code is public on GitHub. It works on phones and computers, can be installed like an app, and keeps working offline for fields already loaded. It is available in English and Spanish. No special equipment is needed, just a phone or computer with internet.

What We Considered
We wanted farmers to trust the answers, so TERRA is honest about its limits. It separates measured data from estimates and labels how confident it is in each plan. Some numbers are less certain than others. Its water estimates for cotton and guar run higher than published field studies, and satellite images can miss details on small fields. Money estimates depend on future prices nobody can predict.

We also wanted it to be usable by any farmer, not only tech-savvy ones. The language is plain, it runs on a phone, and it works in Spanish, which many Arizona farm families speak.

Intended Impact
TERRA is meant to help farmers use less water without losing their income. It gives them a way to compare plans before they plant, using the same evidence a researcher would look at. We still encourage farmers to check plans against their own soil tests, local markets and their extension agent. TERRA doesn’t make the decision for them. It makes sure they have good information when they do.

Arizona is facing the dry future first, and other farming regions are not far behind. By turning NASA’s view of Earth into something useful on the ground, Team ExtraTerra hopes to help farms here and elsewhere keep going as water gets harder to find.
